stories.headline: U.S. strikes Iran again as Tehran fires missiles and drones across region
stories.dek: The U.S. military struck targets in Iran on Tuesday, and Iran responded with missiles and drones as fighting resumed after a month without military action, according to NPR and…
stories.body:
The U.S. military struck targets in Iran on Tuesday, and Iran responded with missiles and drones as fighting resumed after a month without military action, according to NPR and The Hindu. U.S. Central Command said it targeted Iranian military sites including air defense sites, radar systems and maritime assets. The command said the strikes followed attempted Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and on American forces in the region.

Trump said the U.S. hit Iranian radars. "They tried to rebuild their radar because they can't see anything," he told Fox News, according to NPR and The Hindu. He later wrote on social media that if Iran retaliated, "they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level." Late Tuesday, NPR reported, Trump said he would not force Iran to the bargaining table and wrote, "I couldn't care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement."

Iran then launched ballistic missiles at Jordan, NPR reported, citing the Iranian Revolutionary Guard and Jordan's military. Jordan said it shot down 10 missiles and that three landed in unpopulated areas. NPR also reported that Kuwait said it intercepted drone attacks and that Bahrain said all attacks were intercepted after Iran said it had launched drones at U.S. forces there. CBS said Iran launched attacks on Jordan and Bahrain as hostilities flared.

Iranian state media said U.S. strikes hit civilian sites along Iran's southern coast, including Jiroft Airport and sites on Qeshm Island and in Hormozgan province, according to NPR and The Hindu. The outlets gave different casualty figures for a strike on a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak: NPR said Ahmad Nafisi, Hormozgan Province's deputy governor, told Iranian state television that five people, including a child, were killed and at least 68 were wounded, while The Hindu reported Nafisi said two were killed and at least 20 were wounded. Capt. Tim Hawkins, a U.S. Central Command spokesperson, told NPR the U.S. military was aware of the civilian casualty reports, said they originated from Iranian state media, and said, "The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC."

The renewed fighting has pushed oil and gasoline prices higher, NPR and The Hindu reported. Both said crude was already up about 7% this week and more than 50% this year, and AAA put the average U.S. price of regular gasoline at $4.10 a gallon overnight, up from $3.19 a year earlier.
stories.so_what: For ordinary readers, the renewed attacks are already showing up in higher fuel prices as fighting around the Strait of Hormuz threatens a key oil shipping route.

stories.headline: Trump suggests renaming Strait of Hormuz the 'Trump Strait'
stories.dek: President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the "Trump Strait."
stories.body:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait.” In a Truth Social post, Trump wrote: “Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!”

The post followed other Trump-backed name changes. CNBC, The Hindu and SCMP said it came about a week after Trump ordered Lake Ontario renamed “Lake America.” CNBC said Trump earlier declared the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” CNBC said it was not immediately clear how Trump would try to make a name change in a strait that is not near the United States.

Trump’s comment landed as fighting around the strait continued. Axios reported the U.S. military struck Iranian targets on Larak Island to stop what CENTCOM called an “imminent threat” of sea mines in the waterway. Axios also reported Trump and senior aides were considering limited strikes to stop Iran from rebuilding radar and missile capabilities in the strait. A White House official told Axios that “The President retains all options at his disposal.”

The sources differed on who controls the waterway and how open it is. CNBC said Trump and his administration have repeatedly insisted Iran has lost control over the strait, while transits remain below prewar levels. The Hindu said Iran has “effectively shut down” the chokepoint, while The Hill said the waterway does not have a single owner. CNBC said Energy Secretary Chris Wright told the outlet that more than 17 million barrels of oil transited the strait on Monday, versus around 20 million barrels per day before the war started on Feb. 28. The New York Times reported two more oil tankers were attacked near Oman on Monday and oil prices rose more than 2 percent.
stories.so_what: Any new disruption in the strait can raise fuel and shipping costs because the route carries a large share of global oil trade.
stories.what_now: Axios reported Trump had not approved the proposed limited strikes as of last week, but officials said Iran's ballistic missile attacks on U.S. bases in Jordan on Sunday could change his decision.

Al Jazeera reported the spread of Ukrainian drone activity is raising questions about whether Russian airspace could become effectively off limits for more airlines. Its report said that would matter for carriers because Russian routes can shorten flight times between Europe and Asia, while avoiding them can mean longer trips and higher costs.

The sources did not report a formal aviation closure order in Russia tied to Zelenskyy's remarks. They described a warning from Kyiv as fighting expands in the air and both sides signal more attacks.

stories.headline: USS Abraham Lincoln reaches Thailand for first port call in nine months
stories.dek: The USS Abraham Lincoln arrived at Thailand's Laem Chabang port on Wednesday for its first port call in nine months, according to Euronews and The Hindu.
stories.body:
The USS Abraham Lincoln arrived at Thailand's Laem Chabang port on Wednesday for its first port call in nine months, according to Euronews and The Hindu. Euronews said the carrier had been at sea for 286 days, while the Guardian described the deployment as more than 270 days and used 270 days in its headline. Tugs guided the carrier into port, Euronews reported, and the sailors and Marines are headed for Pattaya before the ship departs on Sunday.

The Lincoln has been at the centre of controversy in the United States over conditions on board. Euronews reported Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation after reports of food shortages, broken plumbing and mental health crises. Euronews and the Guardian both said reports included attempted suicides. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said in mid-August that "a small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life," and blamed the media for "trying to paint our warriors as victims," according to Euronews.

The ship left California in November 2025, Euronews said, and was rerouted from duty in the South China Sea to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago. The Hindu said the carrier was involved in the U.S. naval blockade and combat operations in the war with Iran. Rear Admiral Robert Loughran said the stop in Laem Chabang gives sailors and Marines a "well-deserved opportunity" to rest and recharge. Captain Dan Keeler called it the first port visit of a "historic deployment."

Thai authorities said they had prepared for the arrival in Pattaya. The Guardian reported that about 600 officials would provide security and other assistance, citing provincial governor Narit Niramaiwong. Euronews said Pattaya mayor Poramase Ngampiches said buses had been arranged to take sailors between the ship and the resort, with officials focused on safety and fair pricing. He also said sailors were banned from water sports such as jet skis and from using Thailand's cannabis laws, according to Euronews.
stories.so_what: For ordinary readers in Pattaya, the arrival means thousands of visiting U.S. personnel, tighter security and a short burst of business for local transport, shops and nightlife venues.
stories.what_now: Pattaya mayor Poramase Ngampiches said buses will carry sailors to and from the ship until the carrier departs on Sunday.

stories.headline: Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second Hong Kong security law case
stories.dek: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security, in his second prosecution…
stories.body:
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security, in his second prosecution under Beijing's 2020 national security law. Euronews and the Guardian reported Wong, 29, entered the plea at Hong Kong's high court. Sky News said the charge could see him sentenced to life in prison.

Prosecutors said Wong worked with exiled activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against Hong Kong and China. Euronews reported prosecutors said Wong supported those efforts from Hong Kong through foreign and social media, including sharing Law's posts and an online petition urging digital forensic companies to stop cooperating with police. The New York Times said Wong was accused of urging Western politicians including Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio to pressure Hong Kong by imposing sanctions on the city.

Wong is already serving four years and eight months after pleading guilty in a separate national security case linked to an unofficial primary election, according to Euronews. The Guardian said he has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020, had spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027. Both outlets said this is his second prosecution under the law, and the Guardian said he is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under it.

Wong wore a blue shirt in court, according to Euronews and the Guardian. The Guardian said he waved at supporters and stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty. Outside court, people queued overnight for seats, the Guardian reported. A supporter who asked not to be named told the Guardian, "Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong's plea is a forced reality." Before the hearing, Euronews reported, a supporter shouted, "Hang in there" to Wong.
stories.so_what: The plea is likely to keep one of Hong Kong's best-known democracy activists in prison beyond his expected January 2027 release.
stories.what_now: Wong is expected to be sentenced later.

stories.headline: Germany blames Russia for attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
stories.dek: Germany said on Tuesday that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.
stories.body:
Germany said on Tuesday that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month. Authorities found a drone loaded with explosives near a Ukrainian plane on Aug. 4 and defused it, according to NPR. DW reported authorities found the device in the airport security area between Ukrainian cargo aircraft and said investigators believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby. DW also said German media reported a third explosive-laden drone was later discovered at the airport.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were "known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine," according to NPR. He said police investigations, crime patterns and intelligence findings showed that people acted on behalf of Russian state entities. Dobrindt also said Germany should expect further hybrid attacks by Russia.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said the case was part of a "long series of destabilization operations" against Europe, DW reported. He announced tighter entry controls for Russian nationals, plans to seek more European Union sanctions listings tied to hybrid attacks, and more pressure on Russia's "shadow fleet," NPR reported. He also said Germany would coordinate its response with EU and NATO partners.

Russia rejected the accusation. NPR reported Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova called it a "far-fetched and contrived pretext" and said Berlin had presented no convincing evidence. Putin said Germany was using the incident to distract from domestic failings and told reporters in Kyrgyzstan, "But where is the proof? Well, the proof has been planted," according to NPR and DW.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said after speaking with Chancellor Friedrich Merz that "NATO stands in full solidarity with Germany," NPR and DW reported. DW said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called Germany's steps "strong measures" and said "hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response."
stories.so_what: The case points to a security threat at a major German freight hub that supports Ukraine and NATO transport operations.
stories.what_now: Germany said the Russian consulate in Bonn will close effective Sept. 18.

stories.dek: China and Egypt are holding joint air force drills in Egypt under the name "Eagles of Civilisation," in a move the sources describe as a sign of Beijing's expanding reach.

China and Egypt are holding joint air force drills in Egypt under the name "Eagles of Civilisation," in a move the sources describe as a sign of Beijing’s expanding reach. According to the South China Morning Post, Chinese J-16 fighters flew to Egypt recently and were supported by YU-20 tankers that refuelled them in the air.

The SCMP said the exercise includes Chinese jets operating alongside Egyptian Rafales and MiG-29s. It called the deployment the first time China has sent J-16 fighters to Africa, and said it gives China experience in moving a combat force across continents and operating farther from home.

Euronews said the drills come as Egypt and China deepen ties beyond infrastructure and trade into technology, defence and a broader strategic partnership. It reported that Chinese President Xi Jinping returned to Cairo as the two countries pushed their relationship in those areas.

Taken together, the sources portray the exercise as both a military operation and a political signal. The SCMP framed it as evidence that China is beginning to match its economic presence abroad with greater military reach, while Euronews said the wider Egypt-China partnership carries regional implications.

stories.headline: Xi calls for new Middle East security order on Egypt visit
stories.dek: Chinese President Xi Jinping called on Middle East countries to oppose external interference and strengthen regional dialogue on peace and security during talks in Cairo with…
stories.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping called on Middle East countries to oppose external interference and strengthen regional dialogue on peace and security during talks in Cairo with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi on Wednesday. According to China's Xinhua news agency, Xi said “the people of the Middle East are the masters of their own affairs” and said regional countries should consider reshaping the security order. It was Xi’s first visit to Cairo in a decade, Al Jazeera reported.

Xi was greeted by el-Sisi with a 21-gun salute at the Ittihadiya presidential palace. According to a statement from el-Sisi’s spokesperson cited by Al Jazeera, the two leaders discussed the six-month US-Israel war on Iran and urged “diplomatic solutions” to reach a “comprehensive agreement to end the war.”

El-Sisi’s office said the two countries signed an agreement to launch the third phase of the Egyptian-Chinese industrial zone at the Suez Canal. Al Jazeera reported officials say the zone already hosts 200 companies and investments worth about $4bn, though Egypt did not announce a figure for the new investments. A series of additional agreements was also signed, but Egyptian officials did not give details.

Xi said China “stands ready to work with countries in the region to safeguard the security of international shipping lanes, advance development cooperation … and eliminate the breeding grounds for conflict,” according to Xinhua as quoted by Al Jazeera. The Japan Times said Xi was returning to a Middle East “convulsed by war” and facing renewed U.S. economic pressure on Tehran.
stories.so_what: The visit points to deeper Chinese economic and diplomatic involvement in Egypt and the wider Middle East at a time when regional security ties are shifting.

stories.dek: Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation as U.S. Army secretary, the White House confirmed on Monday, August 31, 2026.
stories.body:
Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation as U.S. Army secretary, the White House confirmed on Monday, August 31, 2026. Axios, citing a Department of Defense official, said he is stepping down, and The Wall Street Journal first reported the resignation, according to Axios.

Axios reported two key reasons for Driscoll's decision: he felt his modernization initiatives were being blocked, and he was frustrated by the chaos after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired senior generals. Axios said Driscoll recently spoke with President Trump about his concerns over the state of the Army. A White House official told Axios Driscoll was asked to stay longer, until after midterms, but chose to leave.

The sources describe tension between Driscoll and Hegseth. Axios said Hegseth did not warm to Driscoll, and some U.S. officials told Axios Hegseth was "suspicious and paranoid" toward him, partly because Driscoll was close to Vice President JD Vance, his Yale Law classmate. Axios also cited New York Times reporting that Hegseth allegedly removed four officers from a promotions list after Driscoll refused to do so, and Fox News reporting that Driscoll resisted pressure to fire senior adviser Col. David Butler.

Kelly said Driscoll had been "highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army" and credited him with "outstanding leadership" during military operations and work on Russia-Ukraine negotiations. But Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, blamed Hegseth for the departure, saying, "I do not welcome Secretary Driscoll's resignation... It is far past time for President Trump to recognize the lasting harm that Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense."
stories.so_what: His exit adds to a leadership gap that Axios and The Hindu said leaves the Army without Senate-confirmed civilian or uniformed leadership.

stories.headline: Vance tells Jewish Republicans Israel is key to U.S. security
stories.dek: Vice President JD Vance appeared before the Republican Jewish Coalition at the Venetian hotel in Las Vegas on Monday, where he called Israel "extremely important to America's…
stories.body:
Vice President JD Vance appeared before the Republican Jewish Coalition at the Venetian hotel in Las Vegas on Monday, where he called Israel "extremely important to America's national security" and condemned rising antisemitism, according to two sources familiar with his remarks cited by Axios.

In a 30-minute Q&A with former Minnesota Sen. Norm Coleman, Vance said "Jew hatred is corrosive to the soul" as he recalled talks with the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, Axios reported. Chevron is the only U.S. oil major active in Venezuela through joint ventures with state oil company PDVSA, according to CNBC, and CBS described it as the only U.S. oil company operating there. CBS said Chevron estimates its production cost in Venezuela at about $20 per barrel. But several sources said higher output will take time because infrastructure is badly degraded. stories.headline: LUX-ZEPLIN scientists report lone signal in search for dark matter
stories.dek: Scientists working on the LUX-ZEPLIN, or LZ, experiment said they saw a single particle interaction that could be a sign of dark matter, but they said they are not claiming a…
stories.body:
Scientists working on the LUX-ZEPLIN, or LZ, experiment said they saw a single particle interaction that could be a sign of dark matter, but they said they are not claiming a detection. The BBC reported the finding was presented at a conference in Japan on Tuesday. The Japan Times said researchers in South Dakota observed hints of dark matter during a deep-underground experiment. The New York Times said the lone signal does not fit the profile of any other known particles, according to physicists.

The BBC said the study involved 250 scientists and engineers from 39 institutions in six countries, including researchers from the University of Bristol, over two years. It said the detector is housed at the US Department of Energy's Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, nearly a mile underground.

According to the BBC, the event could potentially have been caused by a Weakly Interacting Massive Particle, or WIMP, a leading dark matter candidate. But the result was rated at 2.6 sigma, below the usual five-sigma threshold for a discovery. "With only one event, we don't want to get ahead of ourselves," Professor Rick Gaitskell of Brown University said, according to the BBC. "We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input."

Dr Sam Eriksen of the University of Bristol told the BBC the signal could be "the first step in understanding dark matter as a particle," though further research could show it is unrelated to dark matter. Professor Henning Flaecher of Bristol said researchers had spent "countless hours" checking for known explanations and that "to date none provide a convincing explanation," the BBC reported.
stories.so_what: If the signal holds up, it could help explain the invisible substance scientists say makes up more than 85% of the universe.

stories.dek: Nepal's disaster authority said on September 2 that flash floods on the China-Nepal border had killed at least 1,204 people in Nepal, with 4,216 still missing a week after the…

Nepal's disaster authority said on September 2 that flash floods on the China-Nepal border had killed at least 1,204 people in Nepal, with 4,216 still missing a week after the disaster. The floods devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal after what Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said was an ice-rock avalanche in the Himalayas that sent floodwaters down the Bhotekoshi River into Rasuwa on August 26. Chinese officials, cited by The Hindu, said 21 people were killed in Tibet and 541 were missing there.

According to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 348 bodies were recovered in Chitawan district, 217 in Nawalparasi East, 202 in Nawalparasi West, 155 in Nuwakot, 115 in Rasuwa, 69 in Gorkha, 60 in Dhading and 38 in Tanahu. The authority said 583 of the missing are foreigners. The Hindu reported that 11,993 people have been rescued and about 21,314 security personnel have been mobilised.

Rescue teams from the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force, foreign technical experts and project employees were still searching tunnels and underground powerhouses along the Bhotekoshi river, but The Hindu said they had not located the missing workers there. Euronews reported rescuers had recovered only bodies from tunnels blocked by sludge, though teams were still digging, drilling and blasting through debris. CBS News reported that heavy monsoon rain had swollen the Trishuli River again on Monday, adding danger to the search.

Families of missing people have begun symbolic funerals after searching shelters, mortuaries and hospital walls displaying photographs of unidentified bodies. At Pashupati Aryaghat, dozens of effigies were cremated in a mass funeral on September 2, The Hindu reported. Nepal Police said postmortem and legal identification procedures had been completed for 1,113 bodies, 95 had been handed over to relatives, and details of 911 unidentified bodies had been uploaded to the Nepal Police website.

Shah told Nepal's House of Representatives that the disaster showed the growing risks faced by Himalayan communities because of climate change and that Nepal must present that link "in a strong manner to the international community." Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told Euronews he still hoped some missing people could be found alive, saying, "Miracles do happen."

A federal judge struck down New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act on Monday, ruling that the state cannot enforce the law because it conflicts with federal authority. Chief Judge Brenda Sannes of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York said the law operated in an area “in which the federal interest is so dominant that it cannot be enforced,” according to Inside Climate News.

The law, signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul in December 2024, sought to make fossil fuel companies help cover costs tied to climate change. Inside Climate News said New York aimed to collect $75 billion over 25 years, a fraction of the more than $500 billion the state projects it will need for risks including hurricanes, storms and extreme heat. The Guardian said the money was for projects to help New York pay for climate mitigation and adaptation.

The ruling came in a lawsuit filed in February 2025 by attorneys general from 22 Republican-led states, according to Inside Climate News. Fossil fuel companies and trade groups including the American Petroleum Institute and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce backed the suit, that report said. The New York Times said the court found the measure conflicted with federal law.

Ken Lovett, a senior communications adviser on energy and environment for Hochul, said in an email to Inside Climate News that “taxpayers shouldn’t have to foot the bill for damages caused by polluters” and that officials are reviewing the decision. State Assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowitz, who co-sponsored the legislation, told Inside Climate News, “They didn’t do anything about it, and so when we passed the law, the purpose was to ensure that these corporations pay for some of the costs of the damage that they caused.” Ryan Meyers of the American Petroleum Institute said, “We have consistently argued that climate policy is a federal, not state, issue, and we are pleased that the court agreed.”

Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data cited by the BBC and Sky News. The Met Office said the average mean temperature across June, July and August was 16.5C, the warmest in a dataset going back to 1884.

The BBC reported the summer followed a spring and summer of persistent heat, with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C, beating the previous record of 34 days set in 1995. It also said temperatures of 35C or higher were recorded on 10 separate days, against a previous record of five, and that 37C or higher was recorded on three separate days, also a new record.

According to the BBC, England, Wales and Northern Ireland each broke their summer mean temperature records, while Scotland had its joint-sixth warmest summer on record. The highest temperature recorded this summer was 38.1C at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August. The BBC said that was provisionally the UK's fifth-hottest day on record by maximum temperature.

The BBC said drought was declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds of England, and wildfires caused devastation in parts of the country. It also reported a rapid attribution study from the Met Office that said the average temperature this summer was made around 130 times more likely by human-induced climate change. Dr Mark McCarthy, head of climate attribution at the Met Office, called summer 2026 "remarkable" and said extremes can be expected more often in the future because of climate change.
stories.so_what: The record heat was linked to drought, wildfires and some flash flooding after rain returned in late August, affecting water supplies, health and daily life.

stories.headline: Tyler Robinson pleads not guilty in Charlie Kirk killing case
stories.dek: Tyler Robinson, 23, pleaded not guilty on Tuesday after Utah District Judge Tony Graf sent the Charlie Kirk killing case to trial in Provo, Utah.
stories.body:
Tyler Robinson, 23, pleaded not guilty on Tuesday after Utah District Judge Tony Graf sent the Charlie Kirk killing case to trial in Provo, Utah. Prosecutors say Robinson fatally shot Kirk, 31, in the neck while the Turning Point USA co-founder spoke at an open-air event at Utah Valley University in Orem on 10 September 2025.

Graf ruled there was enough evidence for prosecutors to proceed on aggravated murder, a capital offence in Utah. According to The Hindu and Euronews, the judge said the positions of several people near the canopy area where Kirk was speaking supported an inference that Robinson knew others were nearby when he fired. Prosecutors said Robinson shot from a rooftop more than 400 feet, or 122 metres, away into a crowd of more than 3,000 people. Defence lawyer Staci Visser argued the state was trying to "shoehorn" the case into the aggravated murder law, saying: "There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim. There is zero evidence that there was any action taken towards other people."

Prosecutors told the court they had a "mountain of evidence" linking Robinson to the shooting, including DNA on a bolt-action rifle, a towel and a screwdriver, video from campus, alleged admissions and statements from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs. Ryan McBride said video showed Robinson "dressed to kill" on campus that day. The sources also reported prosecutors cited a handwritten note allegedly saying, "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it," and an engraved round reading, "Hey Fascist! CATCH!" as evidence of political motive. Robinson also faces possible sentencing enhancements if prosecutors prove he targeted Kirk for his political beliefs.

Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, and his parents, Robert and Kathryn Kirk, attended the hearing. In a statement reported by multiple outlets, the family said the ruling marked "an important step" in their "pursuit of justice" and added that Kirk's children "will grow up without their father." Robinson turned himself in a day after the shooting, according to the sources, and appeared in court in a grey suit, sometimes consulting with his lawyers, BBC reported.
stories.so_what: The ruling keeps capital punishment in play, raising the stakes in a case tied to a high-profile campus shooting and alleged political violence.

stories.dek: OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman face 30 new lawsuits tied to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in British Columbia, Canada.
stories.body:
OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman face 30 new lawsuits tied to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in British Columbia, Canada. TechCrunch said the complaints were filed in a California court on Tuesday, while The Verge and the Guardian said they were filed on Wednesday in California federal court. The new plaintiffs include students, teachers and a principal who were in Tumbler Ridge Secondary School during the attack but were not physically shot.

The cases stem from the February 10 shooting. TechCrunch reported that Jesse Van Rootselaar killed her mother and half-brother at home, then went to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School, killed six more people, injured dozens of others and then died by suicide. The Guardian said eight people were killed and dozens wounded, most of them children.

According to TechCrunch and The Verge, the new lawsuits say OpenAI gave the shooter "substantial assistance and encouragement" and failed to alert Canadian authorities after ChatGPT conversations about gun violence and planning an attack were flagged. The complaints also say OpenAI deactivated Van Rootselaar's account but did not impose a system-wide ban, allowing another account to be created with a different email.

The new filings specifically name OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane as the person the plaintiffs say told staff not to contact authorities, though TechCrunch said the complaints offered no direct evidence he was personally involved. Jason Kwon, OpenAI's chief strategy officer, said in a statement shared with TechCrunch that it was "absolutely false" to say Lehane was involved in the original referral decision or that investigators report to him, and said it was "completely untrue" that safety decisions were driven by "political" or "public relations" factors. Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer for the plaintiffs, told TechCrunch that Lehane and Altman will be "critical witnesses" and that the claims are based in part on the company org chart and the firm's broader investigation.
stories.so_what: The broader case could test when an AI company must warn police about threatening user activity and whether victims who were not shot can still seek damages.

stories.dek: Tiger Woods was banned from driving for five years on Wednesday after changing his plea in Martin County, Florida, over a March rollover crash in Hobe Sound.
stories.body:
Tiger Woods was banned from driving for five years on Wednesday after changing his plea in Martin County, Florida, over a March rollover crash in Hobe Sound. The 50-year-old pleaded no contest to reckless driving and to refusing to submit to a lawful test, according to the Guardian, BBC Sport and Sky Sports. CBS Sports said Woods changed his plea to guilty. BBC Sport said it had corrected an earlier version that wrongly said he had pleaded guilty.

Under the agreement, Woods was adjudicated guilty of willful and wanton reckless driving, a second offense, fined $1,000 and had his driver's licence suspended for five years, the Guardian reported. He was also fined $500 on the test-refusal count, and court records showed he paid $2,131.44 in fines and costs, the Guardian said. Sky Sports reported Judge Darren Steele told Woods: "There are no exceptions. If you were to drive for any reason at all, you would go immediately back to jail."

The original charge was driving under the influence with property damage, according to the Guardian. Authorities said Woods was driving a Land Rover that overturned after trying to pass a truck towing a trailer on a narrow two-lane road shortly before 2pm on 27 March, Martin County sheriff John Budensiek said, as reported by the Guardian. Woods was alone, got out through the passenger side and was not injured. He told officers he had looked down at his phone to change the radio station when the collision happened, the Guardian, BBC Sport and Sky Sports reported.

A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but he refused a urine test for drugs, the Guardian and BBC Sport said. The Guardian said Woods told investigators he had taken several medications earlier that day, including drugs for high blood pressure and cholesterol, ibuprofen and Vicodin. BBC Sport reported that authorities later said two white pills found in his pocket were identified as hydrocodone. After the arrest, Woods said he would step away from golf "to seek treatment and focus on my health," according to the Guardian and BBC Sport.
stories.so_what: The plea ends the criminal case from the March crash, but Woods cannot legally drive for five years and would risk jail if he does, Sky Sports reported.

stories.dek: A Las Vegas jury on Monday convicted Duane "Keffe D" Davis of orchestrating the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur.
stories.body:
A Las Vegas jury on Monday convicted Duane "Keffe D" Davis of orchestrating the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur. Davis, 63, was found guilty of a single count of murder with a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison, according to both The Hindu and Euronews.

The outlets said jurors deliberated for less than three hours after a trial that lasted nine days. The 16-member panel, including four alternates, heard from 24 prosecution witnesses and three defence witnesses. After the verdict, Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur, cried and hugged prosecutors, while Davis' son covered his face with one hand.

Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors Davis got a gun and "went hunting" for Shakur and Marion "Suge" Knight after Davis' nephew was beaten earlier that night. "He is responsible of the murder of Tupac Shakur," Palal said. Prosecutors said Davis placed himself in the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired and, though he did not pull the trigger, called for the gunfire. Defence lawyer Michael Sanft said there was no physical evidence tying Davis to the shooting and argued Davis' memoir and public statements were "dramatised bravado" made for money.

Shakur was shot in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, when a white Cadillac pulled up beside the car he was riding in at a red light, the sources said. He died six days later. Knight was wounded but survived. Prosecutors said the state would dismiss a gang enhancement charge due to witness logistics. Euronews reported Davis is expected to appeal, and said Shakur's family was waiting until sentencing, which is scheduled for October, before commenting.
stories.so_what: The verdict closes one of the highest-profile unsolved killings in music and could send Davis to prison for life.

stories.body:
Ukraine's Minister for Youth and Sport, Matvii Bidnyi, said motorsport's governing body the FIA was wrong to lift its ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors. Speaking to BBC Sport, he said: "The reasons why Russia was banned from international sports competition have not disappeared. Nothing changes and it became even worse."

Bidnyi said Kyiv's central rail station had been bombed by a Russian drone on Wednesday about an hour before he spoke. "The air alert was just turning off," he said. "Our kids, we all came from the bomb shelter. These attacks continue almost every day." He said Russia "continues full-scale aggression against Ukraine" and that Belarus can still provide military support to Russia.

The FIA ban was imposed in February 2022 after Vladimir Putin ordered the invasion of Ukraine. BBC Sport reported that the FIA's world motorsport council lifted it on 3 August, following what the FIA said was an IOC announcement on 7 July and similar updates by other sports federations. The FIA said it has updated requirements for Russian and Belarusian drivers, national teams, competitors and officials, but still bans events and competitions in Russia and Belarus and "continues to monitor the situation closely in Ukraine".

Bidnyi said other sports bodies, including World Athletics, had not taken the same step. He called the FIA decision "a massive disappointment for everyone in Ukraine" and said it undermined pressure on "the aggressor". He added: "In Russia, elite sport is deeply connected with the military and state propaganda system. It's one of the biggest whitewashing mechanisms. This is why we call it sportswashing."

According to the Ukrainian government figures cited by BBC Sport, 775 Ukrainian athletes and coaches have been killed since Russia's full-scale invasion, including three competitors in the Ukrainian Automobile Federation, and more than 925 sports facilities have been destroyed. BBC Sport said the FIA was contacted for comment and referred to its statement on the policy change.

stories.body:
Bukayo Saka scored the only goal as Arsenal beat Aston Villa and maintained their winning start, with the BBC describing it as a hard-fought Premier League victory for the champions.

The Guardian said Arsenal were authoritative and kept Villa at arm’s length, with David Raya untroubled throughout. It said Unai Emery’s work-in-progress side struggled to test Arsenal despite avoiding the kind of capitulation that can follow successive defeats.

The Guardian highlighted a late defensive moment from Declan Rice, saying his reaction after stopping Ian Maatsen’s run into the box with six minutes of normal time left summed up Arsenal’s satisfaction with the performance.

According to the Guardian, Villa have now lost their first two league matches of a season without scoring for the first time since 2002.
stories.so_what: For readers following the table, Arsenal’s win keeps their early momentum going while Villa are still looking for their first league goal.

stories.headline: Jason Isbell and other musicians sue Suno over AI-generated music
stories.dek: Jason Isbell and three others filed a lawsuit against Suno, accusing the company of training its model on their songs, The New York Times reported.
stories.body:
Jason Isbell and three others filed a lawsuit against Suno, accusing the company of training its model on their songs, The New York Times reported. CBS said Isbell, Guy Forsyth and other musicians filed a class action lawsuit against the AI music platform.

The artists say Suno used their music to train its model without permission, according to CBS. The New York Times said the plaintiffs accuse the company of unlawful imitation, saying Suno’s A.I. imitates their voices.

The lawsuit could test a new legal approach to challenges over A.I.-generated music. The New York Times reported that the case is not based on copyright claims, but on unlawful imitation.

The sources did not provide further details from the complaint or any response from Suno.
stories.so_what: The case could affect how musicians try to stop A.I. systems from copying recognizable styles or voices even when copyright law may not directly apply.

stories.headline: King Charles, Macron and Burnham to preview Bayeux Tapestry display
stories.dek: King Charles III is due to view the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum with French President Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Andy Burnham, according to the BBC and DW World.
stories.body:
King Charles III is due to view the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum with French President Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Andy Burnham, according to the BBC and DW World. The BBC said the British and French leaders will see the exhibition of the historic Bayeux Tapestry at the museum.

DW World reported Macron is on a shorter visit to the UK than the 11th century tapestry's loan period and said he will view the artwork with King Charles and Prime Minister Andy Burnham on his arrival. The New York Times said the monarch was invited to see the embroidery before the museum's major exhibition.

The New York Times said the visit comes almost 40 years after Charles saw the tapestry in France with Diana. DW World described the work as an ancient artwork from the 11th century, while the BBC called it the historic Bayeux Tapestry.

The sources differ on emphasis but all report the same preview visit involving Charles and the tapestry at the British Museum. DW World and the BBC also said Macron and Burnham will attend.
stories.so_what: The preview puts a rare loan of a famous medieval work at the center of a high-profile UK visit involving both British and French leaders.
stories.what_now: The leaders are expected to attend the British Museum preview of the Bayeux Tapestry display.

stories.headline: Wendell Berry, writer and farmer from Kentucky, dies at 92
stories.dek: Wendell Berry, the Kentucky-born author, poet, novelist, essayist and farmer, has died at 92, according to the Guardian and NPR.
stories.body:
Wendell Berry, the Kentucky-born author, poet, novelist, essayist and farmer, has died at 92, according to the Guardian and NPR.

The Guardian reported that Mary Berry, his daughter, confirmed on Monday that he died at his home in Port Royal, Kentucky. NPR said Berry was a beloved American poet, novelist, essayist and farmer.

According to the Guardian, Berry celebrated the farming communities of his native Kentucky in poems, stories, novels and essays. The Guardian said he also warned of the excesses and misjudgments of an industrial, commercialized society.

NPR described Berry as a beloved writer and environmentalist. The Guardian called him an author and agrarian.
stories.so_what: Berry’s death closes the career of a writer whose work linked literature, farming and environmental criticism for readers in the United States.

stories.headline: Met cancels John Galliano exhibit and Met Gala theme after backlash
stories.dek: The Metropolitan Museum of Art is canceling a planned exhibit honoring British designer John Galliano, according to NPR and CBS News.
stories.body:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art is canceling a planned exhibit honoring British designer John Galliano, according to NPR and CBS News. NPR reported the museum will no longer give Galliano a career retrospective, and CBS said the decision followed widespread controversy over plans to highlight his work.

NPR reported that Galliano also will not be celebrated at this year's Met Gala. One NPR report said the museum was canceling an exhibit honoring him, while another said it had canceled both the exhibit and the Met Gala theme tied to him.

The backlash centered on Galliano's past antisemitic and racist statements, according to NPR and CBS. CBS described the reaction as widespread controversy, and NPR said the planned exhibit had led to backlash because of those past comments.

The sources describe Galliano as a British designer and a famed fashion designer. The museum's move reverses plans to honor him at one of fashion's highest-profile institutions and events.
stories.so_what: People who follow the Met Gala and the museum's fashion programming will now see a major planned tribute scrapped after objections to the designer's record.

Euronews said the carnival celebrated British Afro-Caribbean culture with music, dancing and colourful costumes in west London.

The BBC said the three-day event saw dancers in extravagant outfits parading the streets of west London to celebrate Caribbean arts and culture.

Both reports showed the annual carnival as a public celebration centred on parade performances, music and dance for the 60th anniversary event.
